title: Cookie-consent interface friction changes data-sharing choices and time cost
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34025; field experiment randomizing cookie-consent banners plus structural analysis of site-specific and browser-level consent
geography: Comparative online consumer and website setting; policy and interface experiment

observations.period: 2025 working paper; field-experiment and structural-model results

denominator.unit: online users and consent-banner interactions; exact experiment denominator is source-specific

baseline_acceptance.unit: share accepting all cookies absent design manipulation

extra_click_effect.value: shifts users toward more accessible alternatives
extra_click_effect.unit: observed effect of placing options behind extra clicks

explicit_choice_gap.value: many users dismiss banners without making an explicit choice

browser_level_time_cost.value: browser-level consent has larger modeled welfare gains than optimizing site-specific design because it eliminates repeated decisions

observations.method: Field experiment randomizing cookie-consent-banner design, defaults, and site-versus-browser-level consent, combined with survey evidence on understanding and a structural model of consumer surplus and repeated decision time.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not disclose the full experiment denominator or all site/user sample details. Observed acceptance and dismissal are not informed consent, privacy protection, data-use comprehension, or durable welfare. The browser-level and default recommendations are structural-model outputs and depend on assumptions about preferences, time costs, and data value.
observations.subgroup: Online users, consent-banner/interface conditions, and site-specific versus browser-level consent; effects should not be generalized to all websites, devices, accessibility contexts, or privacy regimes.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower acceptance rate can reflect confusion, fatigue, or nonresponse rather than a deliberate privacy choice. Browser-level consent may reduce repeated effort but can also hide meaningful site-specific differences or reduce access to services that depend on data sharing.

boundary: This record adds an interface-friction and repeated-attention-cost mechanism to the platform/data lane. It does not establish informed consent, actual privacy protection, U.S. population generalization, downstream fraud or welfare, or durable platform exit.
